name: BillSum
summary: 3,269 bills from the 103rd to 115th Congress, each with the summary a Congressional Research Service analyst wrote for it.
overview:
BillSum is a summarization benchmark whose documents are law in the making and whose reference summaries were written by professional analysts for their own readers. Bills introduced in Congress are read by legislative analysts at the Congressional Research Service, who write a plain summary of what each one would do; Congress.gov publishes those summaries beside the bill. Anastassia Kornilova and Vladimir Eidelman of FiscalNote paired 22,218 bills from the 103rd to the 115th Congress with those summaries and released the result at the 2019 EMNLP workshop on new frontiers in summarization. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523) and [Congress.gov description of its summaries](https://web.archive.org/web/20210225033348/https://www.congress.gov/legislation/about)

The corpus was built to be harder than news summarization in a specific way. Bills are written as amendments to existing law, so a section often says only which words of which statute to strike and what to insert; understanding the change means knowing the law it edits. They are also deeply nested, numbered by section, subsection, paragraph, and clause, which makes sentence boundaries unclear and defeats the sentence-level assumptions of extractive systems. The authors therefore kept mid-length legislation, 5,000 to 20,000 characters, and measured length in characters rather than words because bill structure makes word counts inconsistent. They also report that the analysts often paraphrase rather than quote, so the summary is not assembled from sentences of the bill. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523)

The original results were extractive. An oracle that picks the best sentences of a bill reached 45.11 ROUGE-1, 28.74 ROUGE-2, and 37.38 ROUGE-L on this test split, while the authors' best system, a BERT classifier over sentences with document and summary features, reached 40.80/23.83/33.73. Pre-trained sequence-to-sequence models then overtook that comfortably: PEGASUS reported 57.31/40.19/45.82 in its paper and 59.67/41.58/47.59 for a later checkpoint, and reported 44.78/26.40/34.40 after fine-tuning on only 100 bills, which already beat the extractive state of the art on ROUGE-2. BillSum remains a standard long-document summarization benchmark and is a common test of how well a model handles legal and legislative prose. [PEGASUS paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08777) and [reported checkpoint scores](https://github.com/google-research/pegasus/blob/main/README.md)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official US test split: 3,269 bills with their reference summaries, as published in `us_test_data_final_OFFICIAL.jsonl` inside the authors' `billsum_v3.zip`. The 18,949-bill training split and the separate 1,237-bill California test split are not imported; the California bills are summarised by a different body under different conventions and the authors treat them as an out-of-distribution transfer set. The archive carries no version history, so it is pinned by its SHA-256 digest, and the importer refuses to write if the download does not match. The split covers the 103rd to the 115th Congress, from 171 bills for the 104th to 297 for the 114th, and holds 2,088 House bills and 1,181 Senate bills. [Data documentation](https://github.com/FiscalNote/BillSum/blob/master/BillSum_Data_Documentation.md)

Each Task Prompt asks for a summary of one bill, names the bill and the Congress that received it, and then gives the bill text in full, in a fenced block. The text is reproduced exactly as published, including its fixed-width legislative layout and the typesetter's doubled quotation marks around amended language, which is why it is fenced rather than reflowed. Texts run from 5,004 to 19,998 characters, averaging 10,268, which is the mid-length band the corpus was filtered to.

The Solution is the analyst's summary, reproduced verbatim as a single piece of prose. Summaries run from 62 to 4,986 characters, averaging 1,184; about half are one paragraph and the rest are broken into short paragraphs that follow the bill's divisions. Keys are the upstream bill identifiers, such as `106_hr2724`, which name the Congress and the bill number, and tasks are ordered by Congress, then chamber, then number.

The importer uses only Python's standard library. It checks the digest of the archive, that the split holds exactly the expected number of bills from each Congress and chamber, that every bill identifier parses and is unique, that no bill is missing its text, title, or summary, and that the character counts the records carry match the text they describe. It can be rerun with python3 data/billsum/import.py.
scoring:
BillSum is scored with ROUGE against the single reference summary: the authors report ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F-scores, chosen because F-scores "encourage a balance between comprehensiveness and conciseness", with precision and recall reported separately in an appendix. There is no official scoring script in the repository and no leaderboard, and the paper does not name a ROUGE implementation or state its stemming and stop-word settings, so published numbers come from each paper's own configuration. The authors capped generated summaries at 2,000 characters, the length at or below which 90% of the reference summaries fall, and note that filling that budget favours recall over precision, so a comparison between systems is only meaningful when their output lengths match. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523)

The authors also report an oracle: the ROUGE a system would obtain by choosing, with knowledge of the reference, the best sentences of the bill. On this split the oracle reaches 45.11 ROUGE-1, which bounds what a purely extractive system can do and sits below what later abstractive models reached, because the analysts paraphrase rather than quote. Published numbers for the US test split and the California test split are not comparable to each other. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523)

Benchopedia stores the bills and their reference summaries. It does not run ROUGE or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
One reference summary per bill, scored with ROUGE, measures agreement with one professional's wording rather than whether a summary is right. The analysts write for congressional readers in a house style that leads with the verb of the amendment, so a summary that is accurate but differently organised scores poorly, and there is no human evaluation or agreement study in the paper to calibrate that. With no official scoring script, differences between ROUGE implementations, stemming choices, and output-length caps can exceed the differences between systems. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523)

The corpus is a filtered slice of legislation, not a sample of it. Bills outside 5,000 to 20,000 characters were dropped, along with near-duplicates above 96% similarity, which leaves about 20% of the bills of the period; omnibus and appropriations bills, the longest and arguably the most consequential, are therefore absent, and the authors say that treating them is future work. Bills sharing a title were all placed in the training split, so the test split is not a random sample of what remains. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00523)

The texts are the formatted documents of the period, which shows in the data: eleven records carry stray control characters left by the original typesetting, and a few summaries contain characters that were mangled when the file was encoded. Each is kept as published rather than repaired. The bills are also US federal legislation in English from 1993 to 2018, drafted in a particular legal idiom, so performance here says little about legislative text from other jurisdictions or in other languages.

The bills and their summaries have been published on Congress.gov since they were introduced, and this split has been distributed since 2019 and carries no canary string, so a model may have read these documents, these summaries, or the split itself in training. There is no held-out portion that avoids this.
